message:
QUESTION:
Which production line has the worst defect performance, and did the switch to the new resin supplier on Lines 2 and 3 increase defects?

DATA:
Injection-moulding plant, three lines making the same part. Four weeks of production.

| Line | Weeks 1-2 units | Weeks 1-2 defects | Weeks 3-4 units | Weeks 3-4 defects |
| Line 1 | 10,000 | 150 | 10,000 | 150 |
| Line 2 | 4,000 | 60 | 4,000 | 140 |
| Line 3 | 6,000 | 90 | 6,000 | 150 |

Changes at the start of week 3:
- Lines 2 and 3 switched to resin from a new supplier. Line 1 stayed on the old resin.
- Lines 2 and 3 also replaced manual sample inspection (1 in 10 parts checked visually, with the defect rate extrapolated to the batch) with 100% automated optical inspection. According to the quality engineer, the optical system detects small surface flaws that the manual check often missed. Line 1 kept manual sampling.

Customer returns traced to each line:
| Line | Weeks 1-2 | Weeks 3-4 |
| Line 1 | 14 | 13 |
| Line 2 | 11 | 12 |
| Line 3 | 9 | 10 |

All three lines run the same shift pattern, with the same staffing levels and a similar mix of operator experience.

<analysis>
# Defect Review: Lines 1-3, Weeks 1-4

## Summary

- **Line 1 is not the worst line.** It has the most defects only because it makes the most parts. Its defect rate is no higher than the other lines.
- **Line 2 is the line to watch.** Its customer return rate is roughly double that of Lines 1 and 3, and this was true *before* any change in week 3.
- **This data cannot tell us whether the new resin increased defects.** Lines 2 and 3 switched to the new resin and to 100% automated optical inspection in the same week. The optical system is known to catch flaws the manual check missed. The rise in recorded defects could come from the resin, the better inspection, or both. Customer returns did not rise meaningfully.

## Defect rates, not defect counts

Line 1 makes half the plant's output, so it will have the most defects even if it performs well. The right comparison is the defect rate (defects ÷ units).

| Line | Wk 1-2 rate | Wk 3-4 rate | Inspection wk 3-4 | Resin wk 3-4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Line 1 | 1.5% | 1.5% | Manual 1-in-10 sample | Old |
| Line 2 | 1.5% | 3.5% | 100% optical | New |
| Line 3 | 1.5% | 2.5% | 100% optical | New |

In weeks 1-2, when all lines used the same inspection method, all three had the same 1.5% rate. On the comparable measure, no line stood out.

## Why the week 3-4 rise cannot be put down to the resin

Two things changed at once on Lines 2 and 3:

1. **New resin supplier.** This could create more defects.
2. **Switch to 100% automated optical inspection.** This finds more defects, including small surface flaws the manual check often missed.

Line 1 kept both the old resin and manual sampling. So it is not a control for the resin alone. It differs from Lines 2 and 3 in both respects. A higher recorded rate on Lines 2 and 3 is exactly what we would expect from better detection, even if the resin made no difference.

This also means Line 1's steady 1.5% is not good evidence of better quality. Its true rate is probably understated, like the week 1-2 figures on all lines. The 2.5-3.5% now recorded on Lines 2 and 3 may be closer to the plant's real defect level.

## Customer returns

| Line | Wk 1-2 returns (per 1,000 units) | Wk 3-4 returns (per 1,000 units) | 4-week total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Line 1 | 14 (1.4) | 13 (1.3) | 27 (1.35) |
| Line 2 | 11 (2.75) | 12 (3.0) | 23 (2.9) |
| Line 3 | 9 (1.5) | 10 (1.7) | 19 (1.6) |

What the returns show:

- **Returns did not double on Line 2.** They went from 11 to 12, and on Line 3 from 9 to 10. These changes are well within normal week-to-week variation for counts this small. There is no clear sign that more defective parts are reaching customers since the switch.
- **One point is worth checking.** With 100% inspection, flagged parts should be removed before shipping, so returns on Lines 2 and 3 might have been expected to *fall*. They did not. This could mean the new resin produces somewhat more defects that offset the better screening. It could also mean the optical system mainly catches cosmetic flaws that customers don't return parts for. The data cannot separate these.
- **Line 2 stands out in both periods.** Its return rate is about twice that of Lines 1 and 3. At Line 1's rate, Line 2 would have expected about 11 returns over four weeks; it had 23. This gap existed before the resin and inspection changes, so neither change caused it.

Line 2 also has a higher recorded defect rate than Line 3 (3.5% vs 2.5%) despite the same resin and inspection. Together with the returns, this points to something specific to Line 2, such as tooling, machine settings, or how its output is routed to customers. Staffing and shift patterns are the same across lines, so they are unlikely to explain it.

## Recommended actions

1. **Separate the resin effect from the inspection effect.** Any one of these would work:
   - Run the old resin on Line 2 or 3 for a period while keeping optical inspection, and compare defect rates.
   - Run a batch of Line 1 output through the optical system, to get a like-for-like baseline under the old resin.
   - Re-inspect a sample from Lines 2 and 3 using the old manual method, to see what rate it would have recorded.
2. **Categorise the defects the optical system finds.** Split them by type, such as small surface flaws versus functional defects. If the increase is mostly small surface flaws, it most likely reflects better detection.
3. **Investigate Line 2 specifically.** Look at tooling, machine settings, and customer routing to understand why its returns run at about twice the rate of the other lines.
4. **Don't revert the resin or raise a supplier quality notice yet.** Hold off until step 1 shows whether the resin is actually responsible. Keep the new resin under watch in the meantime.
5. **Consider optical inspection for Line 1.** That would put all lines on the same measurement basis, so future comparisons are valid.
6. **Repeat this review after the tests above.** Use defect rates and return rates per unit, not raw counts.

---

### Main changes from the draft

- **Worst line.** The draft named Line 1 based on raw defect counts, which reflect its higher volume. Per unit, Line 1 is no worse than the others. On customer returns, Line 2 is the outlier.
- **Inspection change.** The draft left out that inspection changed at the same time as the resin. It also wrongly claimed that everything else affected all lines equally. Because of this, the defect rise cannot be put down to the resin.
- **Customer returns.** The draft said returns on Line 2 roughly doubled. They went from 11 to 12.
- **Operator skill.** The draft credited Line 1's operators for its stable rate. Staffing and experience are similar across lines, and Line 1's stability is mostly explained by its unchanged, less sensitive inspection method.
- **Actions.** Reverting the supplier, the supplier notice, and operator coaching were not supported by the evidence. They are replaced with tests that can answer the resin question.
</analysis>

<review>
# Review of the Defect Analysis

**Verdict:** The analysis is sound and its main conclusions hold. Every figure I checked is correct. I'd still revise it before circulating, because it misses two caveats that make some claims sound more certain than the data allows.

## What holds up

- **All arithmetic is correct.** Defect rates are 1.5% for all lines in weeks 1-2, then 1.5%, 3.5% and 2.5% in weeks 3-4. Return rates per 1,000 are 1.35, 2.9 and 1.6 over four weeks. Line 2's expected returns at Line 1's rate are 10.8, so "about 11" is right.
- **Using rates instead of raw counts** is the right fix for the "Line 1 is worst" error.
- **The confounding point is correct and is the key insight.** Resin and inspection changed together on Lines 2 and 3, so Line 1 cannot serve as a control for the resin.
- **The Line 2 return gap is real.** 23 returns against about 11 expected is very unlikely to be chance (Poisson p < 0.001). Even against the plant-wide average rate (about 14 expected), it remains significant.
- **The Line 2 vs Line 3 defect gap in weeks 3-4 is real.** 3.5% vs 2.5% under identical resin and inspection gives z ≈ 2.9.
- **The recommendations follow from the evidence.** They focus on separating the two causes before acting.

## Issues to fix

**1. The weeks 1-2 baseline is far less precise than presented. This is the most important issue.**
Manual inspection checked 1 in 10 parts and scaled up the result. So the "60 defects" on Line 2 comes from about **6 actually observed defects**. Line 3's comes from about 9, and Line 1's from about 15.

With counts that small, Line 2's true week 1-2 rate could plausibly be anywhere from about 0.5% to 3.3%. The analysis says all lines had "the same 1.5% rate" and that "no line stood out." That treats noisy estimates as precise. Identical figures from such small samples could also mean the reported numbers were rounded or estimated, which is worth checking.

This matters for two conclusions:
- We can't rule out that Line 2 already had a higher defect rate before the change. That would fit its higher returns.
- The size of the week 3-4 "rise" on each line is uncertain.

**2. Returns lag production.**
Parts returned in weeks 3-4 may have been made in weeks 1-2. So "no clear sign that more defective parts are reaching customers since the switch" is premature. The same lag weakens the point that returns "should have fallen" under 100% inspection. The fix is either to trace returns by production date or to say that weeks 3-4 returns only partly reflect post-change output.

**3. The size of the inspection effect is assumed, not measured.**
The analysis says the higher rates "may be closer to the plant's real defect level." But Lines 2 and 3 rose by different amounts (+2.0 vs +1.0 points) under the same inspection system. So better detection alone doesn't explain the rises cleanly. The analysis notes the Line 2/3 difference later. It would help to link that point here, as further evidence that something beyond inspection is going on, on Line 2 at least.

**4. Minor points**
- "Roughly double" Lines 1 and 3 is fair for Line 1 (2.1×) but a bit generous for Line 3 (1.8×).
- The "Main changes from the draft" section is useful for reviewers. It should be removed if the document goes to a wider audience.
- Recommendation 3 could add one more step: check whether Line 2's returns cluster by customer or by defect type. Returns are the only signal in this data that clearly sets Line 2 apart.

## Suggested wording changes

- Summary bullet 3: add "and weeks 1-2 rates rest on small manual samples, so the size of the rise is uncertain."
- Defect-rates section: replace "no line stood out" with "the sampled rates were similar, but each is based on only 6-15 observed defects."
- Returns section: add "Returns lag production, so weeks 3-4 returns partly reflect parts made before the change."

With these changes, the conclusions stay the same. Line 2 is the line of concern, and the resin question can't be answered yet. The changes just avoid overstating how certain those conclusions are.
</review>

Here is an analysis and a review of it. Produce an improved version.
response:
# Defect Review: Lines 1-3, Weeks 1-4

## Summary

- **Line 1 is not the worst line.** It has the most defects only because it makes half the plant's output. Its defect rate per unit is no higher than the other lines' rates.
- **Line 2 is the line of concern.** Over four weeks its customer return rate was about twice Line 1's and about 1.8 times Line 3's. The gap was already there in weeks 1-2, before the changes. In weeks 3-4, Line 2 also had a higher recorded defect rate than Line 3, even though both used the same resin and the same inspection.
- **This data cannot show whether the new resin increased defects.** Lines 2 and 3 switched to the new resin and to 100% automated optical inspection in the same week. The optical system is known to catch flaws the manual check missed, so the rise in recorded defects could come from the resin, the better inspection, or both. The size of the rise is also uncertain, because the weeks 1-2 rates are based on small manual samples.

## Defect rates, not defect counts

Line 1 makes half the plant's output, so it will record the most defects even if it performs well. The right comparison is the defect rate (defects ÷ units).

| Line | Wk 1-2 rate | Wk 3-4 rate | Inspection wk 3-4 | Resin wk 3-4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Line 1 | 1.5% | 1.5% | Manual 1-in-10 sample | Old |
| Line 2 | 1.5% | 3.5% | 100% optical | New |
| Line 3 | 1.5% | 2.5% | 100% optical | New |

**How precise these figures are.** Under manual sampling, 1 in 10 parts was checked and the result was scaled up to the batch. Each sampled rate therefore rests on a small number of defects actually seen:

| Line | Parts inspected per 2 weeks (manual) | Defects actually observed | Plausible range for true rate (95%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Line 1 | ~1,000 | ~15 | ~0.8% – 2.5% |
| Line 2 | ~400 | ~6 | ~0.5% – 3.3% |
| Line 3 | ~600 | ~9 | ~0.7% – 2.8% |

The weeks 1-2 sampled rates were similar across lines, but each one is imprecise. We cannot rule out that Line 2 already had a higher true defect rate before the change, which would fit its higher returns. All three lines show exactly 1.5%, and Line 1 shows exactly 150 defects in both periods. That is worth checking: it may mean the figures were rounded or estimated rather than counted.

The weeks 3-4 figures for Lines 2 and 3 come from 100% inspection, so they are actual counts (140 and 150) and are much more precise.

## Why the week 3-4 rise cannot be attributed to the resin

Two things changed at once on Lines 2 and 3:

1. **New resin supplier.** This could create more defects.
2. **Switch to 100% automated optical inspection.** This finds more defects, including small surface flaws the manual check often missed.

Line 1 kept both the old resin and manual sampling. It differs from Lines 2 and 3 in both respects, so it cannot serve as a control for the resin. Better detection alone would produce higher recorded rates on Lines 2 and 3 even if the resin made no difference. For the same reason, Line 1's steady 1.5% is not good evidence that its quality is better. Its true rate is probably understated.

However, better detection does not explain the pattern neatly. Lines 2 and 3 had the same resin and the same inspection, yet Line 2 rose by about 2.0 percentage points and Line 3 by about 1.0. The weeks 3-4 difference between them (3.5% vs 2.5%) is unlikely to be chance (z ≈ 2.9). So something specific to Line 2 is adding defects. It could be an existing Line 2 problem, or the new resin behaving worse on Line 2's tooling or settings. The data cannot tell these apart. Line 3's smaller rise could plausibly come from better detection alone, but given how imprecise its baseline is, that is not certain.

## Customer returns

| Line | Wk 1-2 returns (per 1,000 units) | Wk 3-4 returns (per 1,000 units) | 4-week total (per 1,000) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Line 1 | 14 (1.4) | 13 (1.3) | 27 (1.35) |
| Line 2 | 11 (2.75) | 12 (3.0) | 23 (2.9) |
| Line 3 | 9 (1.5) | 10 (1.7) | 19 (1.6) |

**Caveat: returns lag production.** Parts returned in weeks 3-4 may have been made in weeks 1-2. The weeks 3-4 column therefore only partly reflects output made after the change, and the conclusions below about the change are provisional until returns are traced to production dates.

What the returns show:

- **Line 2's return rate is high, and this is not chance.** At Line 1's rate, Line 2 would have expected about 11 returns over four weeks. It had 23 (Poisson p < 0.001). Even against the plant-wide average rate (about 14 expected), the excess is statistically significant. The gap appears in both periods, so the week 3 changes did not cause it, though the lag means some weeks 3-4 returns are pre-change parts anyway.
- **No sign yet of a rise in returns after the switch.** Returns on Line 2 went from 11 to 12 and on Line 3 from 9 to 10. These differences are well within normal variation for counts this small. Because of the lag, this is not yet strong evidence either way about the new resin.
- **Returns did not fall on Lines 2 and 3, which is worth watching.** Under manual sampling, about 90% of defective parts were never inspected and could ship. Under 100% optical inspection, flagged parts should be removed before shipping, so returns would be expected to fall. They did not. There are three possible explanations, which the data cannot separate: the lag (most weeks 3-4 returns may be pre-change parts), the optical system mainly catching cosmetic flaws that customers don't return parts for, or the new resin causing defects that the optical system doesn't detect. A few more weeks of returns, traced by production date, will help settle this.

Taken together, the higher returns and Line 2's higher weeks 3-4 defect rate point to something specific to Line 2, such as tooling, machine settings, or which customers its output is routed to. Staffing, shift patterns and operator experience are similar across lines, so they are unlikely explanations.

## Recommended actions

1. **Separate the resin effect from the inspection effect.** Any one of these would work:
   - Run the old resin on Line 2 or Line 3 for a period while keeping optical inspection, and compare defect rates.
   - Run a batch of Line 1 output through the optical system to get a like-for-like baseline under the old resin.
   - Re-inspect a sample from Lines 2 and 3 using the old manual method to see what rate it would have recorded.
2. **Categorise the defects the optical system finds.** Split them by type, such as small surface flaws and functional defects. If the increase is mostly small surface flaws, it most likely reflects better detection.
3. **Trace customer returns to production date or lot.** This shows which returns came from parts made after the change, and whether those parts are returned more or less often than earlier ones.
4. **Investigate Line 2 specifically.** Check tooling, machine settings and customer routing. Also check whether its returns cluster by customer or by defect type, since returns are the clearest signal in this data that sets Line 2 apart.
5. **Verify the weeks 1-2 records.** Confirm that the manual defect figures are counts of defects actually observed, not rounded or estimated values.
6. **Don't revert the resin or raise a supplier quality notice yet.** Wait until step 1 shows whether the resin is responsible. Keep the new resin under watch in the meantime.
7. **Consider optical inspection for Line 1.** That would put all lines on the same measurement basis, so future comparisons are valid.
8. **Repeat this review after the tests above.** Use defect and return rates per unit, not raw counts, and include several more weeks of returns traced by production date.

---

*Note on this revision (for reviewers; remove before wider circulation):* This version adds the small-sample precision of the weeks 1-2 baseline, the lag between production and returns, the link between the unequal Line 2/Line 3 rises and a Line 2-specific cause, the statistical support for the Line 2 findings, and three new actions: trace returns by production date, check how Line 2's returns cluster, and verify the manual records. It also corrects "roughly double" to about 2.1× Line 1 and 1.8× Line 3. The main conclusions are unchanged.
